triage.name: Hirschsprung disease
triage.reason: Infant with delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension and chronic constipation; diagnosis reached by history, exam, contrast enema and rectal biopsy.

review_issues: exam: term 'Anal wink reflex' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: More common in males, with a male-to-female ratio of about 4:1
Most cases are diagnosed in infancy, but a small number present in older children or adults

risk_factors.text: Having a sibling with Hirschsprung disease
Presence of associated genetic syndromes (e.g., Down syndrome)

family_history: Hirschsprung disease in a sibling or parent

chief_complaints.text: My baby hasn't passed meconium in the first two days
My child has been constipated since birth
My child has trouble pooping and it comes out in small amounts

hpi.onset: From birth; symptoms are present in the neonatal period
hpi.duration: Since birth, often diagnosed in the first few months of life
hpi.progression: Persistent and worsening constipation; may present with acute obstruction in the newborn period or chronic constipation later
hpi.quality: Crampy abdominal pain and bloating; difficulty passing stool
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; can progress to life-threatening enterocolitis
relieving: Passing a small amount of stool

associated_symptoms.text: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth
Poor feeding and poor weight gain
Explosive, foul-smelling stools after rectal stimulation

pertinent_negatives: Passage of meconium within the first 24 hours of life

atypical.how_it_differs: Very rare; may present with chronic constipation and megacolon, often diagnosed after years of symptoms.
Older children may present with chronic constipation, abdominal distension, and failure to thrive; they may have a history of delayed meconium passage that was overlooked.

general.mild: Well-appearing infant, alert, feeding reasonably well
general.moderate: Mildly fussy, distended abdomen, feeding less well
general.severe: Ill-appearing, irritable or lethargic, poor feeding, visibly distended abdomen
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic, dehydrated, with signs of enterocolitis or shock

findings.finding: Empty rectal vault with no stool palpable

findings.maneuver: Withdraw the examining finger after digital rectal examination
findings.finding: Explosive release of stool and gas
Tight anal sphincter with increased tone

findings.maneuver: Stroke the perianal skin to elicit the anal wink
findings.finding: Contraction of the anal sphincter (anal wink present)
No hard stool in the rectal vault

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for masses and organomegaly
Assess for peritoneal signs with gentle palpation and rebound
Plot weight, length and head circumference on a growth chart

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not exclude Hirschsprung disease; leukocytosis with a left shift suggests Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis.
Mild anemia from poor feeding or chronic inflammation; not specific to Hirschsprung disease.
Hyponatremia from vomiting, poor intake or secretory diarrhea in enterocolitis.
Hypokalemia from vomiting and stool losses; can be profound in enterocolitis.
Metabolic acidosis from dehydration, poor perfusion or enterocolitis.
Prerenal azotemia from vomiting and poor intake.
Rises late in infants; use with BUN and urine output to judge hydration.
Supports enterocolitis when elevated; normal CRP does not exclude it.
Elevated with hypoperfusion or severe enterocolitis.
Congenital hypothyroidism is a treatable cause of neonatal constipation and should be excluded.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging in suspected Hirschsprung disease after plain films

findings.text: Narrow, contracted aganglionic distal segment with a transition zone to dilated proximal colon
Delayed clearance of contrast on the post-evacuation film
Rectosigmoid ratio inverted (rectum narrower than sigmoid)
Sawtooth or irregular contractions in the aganglionic segment
Normal-appearing colon (false negative), especially in the newborn period
Free intraperitoneal air or contrast extravasation suggesting perforation

imaging.study: Abdominal x-ray (supine and upright or decubitus)

findings.text: Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels suggesting distal obstruction
Dilated, fluid-filled colon proximal to a narrowed segment
Nonspecific; used mainly to exclude other causes of vomiting or abdominal distension

imaging.preferred_when: Older infants and children when rectal biopsy is not immediately available

findings.text: Absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex with balloon distension of the rectum
Normal rectoanal inhibitory reflex (argues against Hirschsprung disease)

initial.why: Baseline blood count; leukocytosis with a left shift supports enterocolitis
Assesses dehydration and electrolyte losses from vomiting or diarrhea

initial.test: Abdominal x-ray (supine and upright or decubitus)
initial.why: First study in a neonate with delayed meconium and distension; looks for obstruction or perforation
Shows the transition zone and is the main noninvasive test
Excludes congenital hypothyroidism as a treatable cause of neonatal constipation

confirmatory.why: Reference standard: absent ganglion cells and hypertrophied acetylcholinesterase-positive nerve fibers in the submucosa

supporting.why: Absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex supports the diagnosis
supporting.only_if: rectal biopsy is not readily available or the diagnosis is unclear
fever, lethargy, abdominal tenderness or explosive diarrhea suggests enterocolitis

supporting.why: Assesses perfusion in an ill-appearing infant
Used when suction biopsy is nondiagnostic or unavailable
supporting.only_if: suction biopsy is inconclusive or the child is older

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Rarely needed and adds radiation; contrast enema and biopsy are preferred
Not diagnostic for Hirschsprung disease; reserved for excluding other causes of vomiting or distension
No role in neonatal bowel obstruction
Not needed unless pancreatitis is suspected
Does not help diagnose Hirschsprung disease

decision_points: Any neonate who has not passed meconium within 48 hours should be evaluated for Hirschsprung disease
Signs of enterocolitis (fever, lethargy, abdominal tenderness, explosive diarrhea) require resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent decompression before elective workup
Contrast enema can be normal in the newborn period; a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis, and rectal biopsy is still needed if suspicion remains
Rectal biopsy is the reference standard and should not be delayed when the clinical picture is convincing

differential.name: Meconium plug syndrome
differential.why_considered: Neonate with delayed meconium passage and abdominal distension, the classic Hirschsprung presentation

history: Meconium passed after a single rectal stimulation or enema
Often associated with prematurity, maternal diabetes or magnesium exposure
exam: Distended abdomen that decompresses after passing the plug
imaging: Contrast enema shows a meconium plug with a normal-caliber colon and no transition zone
Contrast study is therapeutic and the infant then stools normally

differential.name: Intestinal atresia
differential.why_considered: Neonate with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension and failure to pass meconium
differential.trigger: Bilious vomiting on the first day of life with a markedly distended abdomen

history: Bilious vomiting from the first day of life
labs: Dehydration and electrolyte derangement from vomiting
imaging: Abdominal x-ray shows dilated proximal bowel with a paucity of distal gas
Contrast enema shows a microcolon with no transition zone

differential.name: Meconium ileus
differential.why_considered: Neonate with delayed meconium, distension and bilious vomiting

history: Failure to pass meconium with progressive distension
exam: Distended abdomen, often with palpable loops of thickened bowel
labs: Sweat chloride or genetic testing confirms cystic fibrosis
imaging: Abdominal x-ray shows a bubbly, ground-glass appearance in the right lower quadrant
Contrast enema shows a microcolon with inspissated meconium pellets

differential.name: Necrotizing enterocolitis
differential.why_considered: Neonate with abdominal distension, feeding intolerance and lethargy
differential.trigger: Premature infant with bloody stools, abdominal wall erythema or pneumatosis on x-ray

labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis
imaging: Abdominal x-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas or pneumoperitoneum

differential.name: Congenital hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Neonate with constipation, poor feeding and abdominal distension

history: Delayed meconium passage but normal stooling once established
exam: Large fontanelle, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hypotonia
labs: Elevated TSH and low free T4 on newborn screen or serum testing
imaging: Thyroid scan may show ectopic or absent gland

differential.name: Functional constipation
differential.why_considered: Older infant or child with chronic constipation and abdominal pain

history: Meconium passed within the first 24–48 hours
Stool withholding behavior, painful stools, soiling
exam: Fecal impaction palpable in the rectal vault
Normal anal tone and no explosive stool on withdrawal
imaging: Abdominal x-ray shows stool throughout the colon without a transition zone
Contrast enema shows a dilated rectum with stool, no aganglionic segment

differential.name: Down syndrome with constipation
differential.why_considered: Children with Down syndrome have a higher risk of Hirschsprung disease and also commonly have functional constipation

history: Constipation may be functional or due to Hirschsprung; delayed meconium still raises suspicion
exam: Rectal exam may show normal tone or tight sphincter
imaging: Contrast enema may be less reliable; rectal biopsy is needed if suspicion is high

severity.mild: Neonate or infant with delayed meconium passage, mild abdominal distension, feeding well, no vomiting, no signs of enterocolitis
severity.moderate: Persistent constipation with abdominal distension, occasional vomiting, poor weight gain, but no systemic illness
severity.severe: Signs of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis: fever, lethargy, abdominal tenderness, explosive diarrhea, dehydration, electrolyte derangements
severity.critical: Toxic-appearing infant with enterocolitis, sepsis, shock, or perforation with peritonitis

red_flags.finding: Fever, lethargy, abdominal tenderness or explosive diarrhea
red_flags.meaning: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis; requires urgent resuscitation, antibiotics and decompression

red_flags.finding: Bilious vomiting with a distended, tense abdomen
red_flags.meaning: Possible intestinal obstruction or perforation; needs urgent surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or tachycardia with poor perfusion
red_flags.meaning: Septic shock from enterocolitis; start fluids and antibiotics immediately

complications.name: Intestinal obstruction
clues: Failure to pass stool or flatus

complications.name: Failure to thrive
clues: Weight loss or poor weight gain

complications.name: Postoperative stricture or adhesion obstruction
clues: Recurrent vomiting and distension after pull-through surgery
Narrowing at the anastomosis on contrast study

special_populations.differences: Most cases present in the neonatal period with delayed meconium passage; contrast enema may be normal in the first weeks of life, so rectal biopsy is often needed.
Older children may present with chronic constipation, abdominal distension and failure to thrive; a history of delayed meconium may have been overlooked.
Very rare; may present with chronic constipation and megacolon, often diagnosed after years of symptoms.

key_questions.question: When did your baby first pass meconium (the first dark stool)?
key_questions.looking_for: Meconium passed more than 48 hours after birth, or not at all; the single most important historical clue

key_questions.question: Has your child ever had a normal stooling pattern, or has constipation been present since birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Constipation dating from birth rather than starting later, which points away from functional constipation

key_questions.question: How often does your child pass stool, and what does it look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Infrequent, small, ribbon-like or pellet stools; straining without result

key_questions.question: Does your child pass a large amount of stool or gas after a rectal thermometer or suppository?
key_questions.looking_for: Explosive release of stool and gas after rectal stimulation, classic for the aganglionic segment

key_questions.question: Has your baby been vomiting? Is it green or bilious?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilious vomiting suggests obstruction and needs urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Is your baby feeding well and gaining weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding, poor weight gain or failure to thrive

key_questions.question: Has your child had fever, lethargy, or sudden foul-smelling diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, which is life-threatening and needs urgent treatment

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have Hirschsprung disease or a similar bowel problem?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history in a sibling or parent, which strongly raises risk

key_questions.question: Does your child have any known genetic conditions such as Down syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Down syndrome or other syndromes associated with Hirschsprung disease

key_questions.question: Has your child had abdominal surgery or any prior bowel problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior surgery or bowel disease that could explain the symptoms

key_questions.question: Is there any blood in the stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Blood in stool argues against Hirschsprung disease and raises concern for other causes

reasoning_points: Delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours of life
Constipation present since birth rather than acquired later
Abdominal distension with an empty rectal vault on digital exam
Explosive release of stool and gas after rectal stimulation
Contrast enema showing a narrow aganglionic distal segment with a transition zone to dilated proximal colon
Rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells and hypertrophied acetylcholinesterase-positive nerve fibers
Exclusion of look-alikes such as meconium plug syndrome, intestinal atresia, meconium ileus and functional constipation
Recognition of enterocolitis as a life-threatening complication requiring urgent treatment

easy: Neonate who has not passed meconium within 48 hours
Classic transition zone on contrast enema
Rectal biopsy confirms absent ganglion cells
medium: Older infant with chronic constipation and failure to thrive
Contrast enema is normal in the newborn period but suspicion remains
Explosive stool after rectal stimulation is the only clue
Family history of Hirschsprung disease in a sibling
hard: Neonate with enterocolitis presenting with fever, lethargy and explosive diarrhea rather than constipation
Child with Down syndrome where constipation is attributed to the syndrome
Older child or adult with long-standing constipation and megacolon
Suction biopsy is nondiagnostic and full-thickness biopsy is needed
